title: Vista Digital Banking
summary: One shared UI language, adapted for four Vista subsidiaries.
text:
2022–2024
Vista Digital Banking
One shared UI language, adapted for four Vista subsidiaries.
My contribution
Delivery scope
Delivery scope: four subsidiaries, English and French, with local currency and regulatory copy. Supported by the project record and ITSS recognition.
One shared UI language, adapted for four Vista subsidiaries.
Vista needed a recognisable banking experience across The Gambia, Guinea, Sierra Leone and Burkina Faso. The UI had to work in English and French while accommodating each subsidiary’s currency, regulatory copy and banking requirements.
UI/UX Designer & Front-End Developer · ITSS · May 2022–April 2024
I helped design corporate and retail banking journeys across the four subsidiaries and built a shared design system that allowed local differences. I designed Vista’s debit card and the screens for its loan application flow. My work also covered onboarding, account views, transfers and approvals within the Temenos Infinity implementation, alongside campaign graphics and HTML/CSS implementation review.
The decisions behind the interface
Keep the design language consistent across subsidiaries. I used shared components and interaction patterns so each local experience remained recognisably Vista, while allowing language, currency and regulatory copy to vary.
Make language available at sign-in. English and French selection sits at the start of the journey, rather than being left inside settings after a customer has already had to log in.
Keep local and company context visible. Currency stays with account balances, and the active legal entity appears beneath the user’s name so corporate users can see which company they are acting for.
Adapt the shared system to corporate banking. Pending approvals have their own counts and prominent placement. Account sorting, filters and custom views support people managing multiple accounts.
What was delivered
The banking design shipped across four localised subsidiaries using one shared system. The work brought a consistent Vista interface to English- and French-speaking markets while preserving the local information customers need.
ITSS’s Most Outstanding Intern of the Year award names my Vista Bank UI/UX work. The four-subsidiary rollout is delivery scope; post-launch usage and task-completion results were not available to me.
Contribution & evidence
At ITSS, I helped adapt one Vista UI design language for four subsidiaries as part of the Temenos Infinity implementation. I designed Vista’s debit card and the screens for its loan application flow. Shared components and interaction patterns provided consistency; language, currency and local requirements shaped each subsidiary’s experience.
Recognition tied to the work
“Your contribution to the Infinity UI/UX design for the Vista Bank Project and Jasper Report Design template differentiated you from your peers.” ITSS · Most Outstanding Intern of the Year, Nigeria Office 6 November 2023
“Your contribution to the Infinity UI/UX design for the Vista Bank Project and Jasper Report Design template differentiated you from your peers.”
The letter recognises my Infinity UI/UX and report-template contributions, together with my commitment and teamwork.
What is shown here
Selected public-facing imagery is shown. Internal implementation screens are omitted to respect confidentiality. The images illustrate the product context; the letter supports the contribution described here.

title: Radius / Pay4Me
summary: Designing cross-border payments for the student and the person paying.
text:
2025
Radius / Pay4Me
Designing cross-border payments for the student and the person paying.
My contribution
Company reported
Radius publishes these as minimum counts (120K+ users and 1,500+ reviews) and an average delivery time. They describe the company, not a measured uplift from my design work. Source: Radius published figures, checked 19 October 2026
Designing cross-border payments for the student and the person paying.
Education and immigration payments have deadlines. A parent or relative may be paying for a student in another country, using another currency.
Product designer · mobile payment experience and marketing site · 2025
I designed sponsored payments, verification, currency visibility, transaction tracking and support. On the website, I organised the information families need before trusting the service enough to install the app.
A personal note
This project changed how I think about payment UX. Sometimes the person making the payment isn’t the person whose future depends on it.
The decisions behind the interface
Give the sponsor a clear payment route. I treated the payer and student as different people in the journey, rather than forcing sponsored payments into a personal transfer.
Put payment constraints before commitment. Currency appears with the balance, and verification status appears with identity, so both are visible before a payment starts.
Build trust before the download. The site uses named institutions, coverage, student testimonials and FAQs, followed by a QR-code handoff to the app.
Use the language of the task. Tuition, SEVIS, WES and visa payments are named directly, with tracking and support easy to reach.
What was delivered
The design connects the website’s trust-building role to the mobile payment journey. Sponsored payments, verification and transaction status are treated as core parts of that experience.
Radius, formerly Pay4Me, reports more than 120,000 registered users, more than 1,500 five-star reviews and average delivery of six hours on business days. These are company-level figures, not results attributed to my design work. Read the published figures .

summary: Making marketplace safety visible from checkout to payout.

Horal
Making marketplace safety visible from checkout to payout.
My contribution
Published product
Google Play lists Horal in the 100+ download band. This is an app-store threshold, not an exact total or a measured design uplift. Source: Horal on Google Play, checked 19 October 2026
Making marketplace safety visible from checkout to payout.
Buyers need to trust independent sellers they may never meet. Sellers need the tools to fulfil those orders reliably.
End-to-end product designer · mobile app and website · 2026
I designed the buyer and seller journeys together: product discovery, store verification, checkout, escrow status and chat, alongside seller onboarding, KYC, inventory, orders and payouts.
The decisions behind the interface
Show who the buyer is dealing with. I placed verification at store level, where buyers assess the seller before paying.
Explain what happens to the payment. I designed escrow around visible stages, from protected payment through delivery confirmation to release of funds.
Connect shopping to fulfilment. Seller stock, orders and wallet tools follow the same transaction lifecycle as the buyer journey.
What was delivered
Horal is live on the web, iOS and Android. The released product includes verified stores, escrow, chat, seller inventory, order management and payouts.
Live releases confirm delivery. The published download count describes product adoption; it does not measure the effect of one design decision.

title: Bizinc
summary: One business profile, with clear control for owners and customers.
text:
2024–2026
Bizinc
One business profile, with clear control for owners and customers.
My contribution
Reported project results
Reported during the redesign period; also +12% service activity. Baselines, dates and measurement methods are unpublished, and individual design causality was not isolated.
One business profile, with clear control for owners and customers.
A business owner needs to manage their identity, services and offers. A customer needs to decide whether that business is right for them. Both journeys meet at the same profile.
UI/UX Intern Product Designer UI/UX Manager · April 2024–May 2026
I mapped owner and customer journeys, designed Business Profile 2.0, marketplace and booking interfaces, and produced reusable components and development handoff. I later led designers and interns as UI/UX Manager.
The decisions behind the interface
Separate management from the public profile. I mapped Business View and Client View separately, then brought them into one shared structure so owner controls stayed out of customer navigation.
Help customers compare before opening a profile. Discovery cards include service information, location, distance and open-now status alongside the route to the business profile.
Connect proposed AI discovery to a real next step. The Bizzy proposal moves from a service request to nearby businesses, availability and booking. It remains proposed work; a prototype confirmation is not a live booking integration.
What was delivered
Bizinc is live. The CEO reference documents my role in rebuilding the platform interface and my progression to UI/UX Manager. Profile requirements, journey maps, wireframes and components show the design work behind it.
Project records report +38% retention, +45% dashboard activation, +23% customer growth and +12% service activity during the redesign period. Baselines and measurement methods are unpublished, so these are reported product results rather than isolated effects of my changes.
Contribution & evidence
I redesigned Bizinc’s platform interface and later led designers and interns as UI/UX Manager. My project work connected business-owner controls with customer-facing profiles, discovery and booking journeys.
“One of his earliest contributions was the complete re-envisioning and redesign of our digital platform.” Michael Fulton II · Chief Executive Officer, Bizinc 9 December 2025
“One of his earliest contributions was the complete re-envisioning and redesign of our digital platform.”
Michael’s letter describes rebuilding the interface from scratch, aligning design work with business goals, and my progression from UI/UX Intern to UI/UX Designer and UI/UX Manager. It also recognises my leadership and delivery under pressure.

title: Kremor AI
summary: Helping people turn a clothing idea into a design that can move toward production.
text:
2024–2026
Kremor AI
Helping people turn a clothing idea into a design that can move toward production.
My contribution
Design & evaluation scope
Three designed surfaces and five operational roles. The founder’s reference supports my design and AI-evaluation responsibilities. Workshop permissions remain to be validated. Source: founder’s reference
Helping people turn a clothing idea into a design that can move toward production.
Someone may know the occasion, textile or feeling they want without knowing how to prompt an AI tool. The generated idea also needs a route into the storefront and garment-production workflow.
UI/UX Designer - Design & Research Lead · Kremor AI · June 2024–July 2026
I led design across the generative workspace, storefront and role-based operations, using one shared system. I also worked on model benchmarking, annotation and qualitative evaluation across complex AI interaction tasks.
The decisions behind the interface
Offer a starting point before asking for a prompt. Quick actions and conversational examples help people describe an idea without specialist design vocabulary.
Name the textiles people are working with. The interface uses Ankara, Aso-Oke, Adire, Kente and Afro-fusion instead of a broad label that loses useful detail.
Connect creative work to operational roles. The design covers the handoff from an approved idea toward production. The five-role workshop permissions model is marked for validation with operating teams.
What was delivered
Three connected product surfaces share one design system. The founder’s reference confirms my combined UI/UX design and AI-evaluation work.
This evaluation work concerned AI outputs, rather than participant usability sessions. The workshop role and permissions model still needs validation.
Contribution & evidence
My contribution combined UI/UX design with AI model evaluation. I worked across the product’s connected surfaces while benchmarking, annotating and reviewing language-model and generative-image output.
“He has demonstrated exceptional expertise in forensic benchmarking, dataset annotation, and qualitative evaluation for both Large Language Models (LLMs) and generative image systems.” Saheed Alabi · Founder, Kremor AI 27 July 2026
“He has demonstrated exceptional expertise in forensic benchmarking, dataset annotation, and qualitative evaluation for both Large Language Models (LLMs) and generative image systems.”

title: Shortlet Lagos
summary: Giving guests and property investors different routes into the same business.
text:
2024
Shortlet Lagos
Giving guests and property investors different routes into the same business.
My contribution
Product & design scope
Product and design scope. ₦50,000 is the designed entry threshold, not a return or adoption metric.
Giving guests and property investors different routes into the same business.
A guest is choosing a place to stay. An investor is deciding what a property share means and what it costs. Combining those decisions would give each audience the wrong information.
Product designer & researcher · 2024
I designed responsive guest-booking and fractional-investment journeys, supported by research into how guests shortlist properties. The two experiences share a visual system while keeping their decisions separate.
The decisions behind the interface
Separate the entry points. Guests begin with stays; investors begin with property investment. Each route introduces the information needed for that decision.
Keep the whole booking query together. Location, check-in, check-out and guest count sit in one search card so the query is visible and editable on mobile.
Explain the investment mechanic first. The investment experience introduces buying shares and the ₦50,000 entry threshold before discussing potential returns.
What was delivered
Shortlet Lagos is live. The design provides distinct booking and investment routes within one responsive product.
The interface shows how the two journeys are separated. Investor comprehension of fractional ownership remains a validation priority.
Live website: https://www.shortlet-lagos.com

title: Synqit
summary: Making a partnership request the starting point for business conversations.
text:
2026
Synqit
Making a partnership request the starting point for business conversations.
My contribution
Reported project result
The design separates three user roles and uses request-first messaging. No quantified improvement is claimed without a published benchmark.
Making a partnership request the starting point for business conversations.
Businesses and Web3 teams were finding potential partners across scattered social channels. Open messaging made it difficult to distinguish a credible partnership from unsolicited outreach.
Lead product designer · end to end · 2026
I interviewed founders, Web3 teams and investors, mapped the information architecture and designed profiles, matchmaking, requests, the dashboard and messaging. I also ran usability testing with businesses to refine the trust signals.
The decisions behind the interface
Let people review a request before a conversation. Messaging unlocks after a partnership request is accepted, giving both sides control over who reaches their inbox.
Make relationship status visible. The dashboard organises requests by pending, accepted and declined so teams can see where each introduction stands.
Design for the three roles in the network. Profiles and journeys account for businesses seeking partners, investors assessing startups and teams managing partnerships.
What was delivered
The designed workflow connects discovery, profile review, request acceptance and messaging. The flow replaces a scattered manual process with explicit steps for each user role.
Discovery speed, partnership quality and acceptance rates still need measurement.

title: Arete
summary: Connecting the steps after a patient finds a doctor.
text:
2026
Arete
Connecting the steps after a patient finds a doctor.
My contribution
Design concept
Design scope across patients, providers, HMO teams and pharmacies. Patient testing is still needed for coverage wording and accessibility.
Connecting the steps after a patient finds a doctor.
A patient’s journey continues through coverage, prescriptions, finding medication and follow-up. Those steps involve different organisations and can leave the patient without a clear next action.
End-to-end product designer · 2026
I designed the connected care journey across patient, provider, HMO and pharmacy experiences. The work covers onboarding, care discovery, consultation, coverage, prescriptions and continued care.
The decisions behind the interface
Keep access possible without insurance details. A Skip for Now route lets the patient continue instead of treating missing coverage information as a dead end.
Design beyond the consultation. The seven-step journey continues into prescriptions, pharmacy access and follow-up rather than stopping at a booking.
Make coverage wording a design priority. Simple, accessible, localised and transparent are the four principles behind the interface. Coverage states must remain understandable without promising an insurer’s approval.
What was delivered
The designs connect seven care steps across four product surfaces, supported by documented requirements, interface states and a shared visual system.
This is documented design work. Coverage comprehension and accessibility still need testing with patients in real conditions.

title: Archi-Tek
summary: Designing a route from an architectural brief to a reviewable output.
text:
2025
Archi-Tek
Designing a route from an architectural brief to a reviewable output.
My contribution
Interaction concept
Designed interaction scope: three fidelity modes and four proposed export formats. The editor is Coming soon; CAD capability remains unverified.
Designing a route from an architectural brief to a reviewable output.
A convincing building image is not the same as a file an architect can revise or hand to an engineer. The interface needs to make the intended output and its limits clear.
Product designer · 2025
I designed prompt entry, design-type selection, generated alternatives, preview and export flows, plus the proposed 3D-editor experience.
The decisions behind the interface
Help people start with a recognisable building brief. Examples such as a three-bedroom bungalow or duplex sit beside the prompt field, with sample designs to show what can be requested.
Let the user choose the output level. Concept Sketch, Schematic Plan and Detailed Model make fidelity an explicit choice rather than leaving the generator to guess.
Keep alternatives and export choices visible. Named design options can be compared before choosing DWG, OBJ, SketchUp or PDF. The proposed editor is labelled Coming soon.
What was delivered
The interface design covers the path from a written brief through comparison, preview and proposed export. The mockups show these interaction decisions.
The editor remains proposed, and editable CAD-export capability has not been verified. The presentation does not imply a working architecture engine.

title: Loan & Investment App
summary: Bringing borrowing and investing together without hiding their differences.
text:
2025
Loan & Investment App
Bringing borrowing and investing together without hiding their differences.
My contribution
Financial app concept
Design scope: five financial products and a designed ₦100,000 investment minimum. Adoption and financial outcomes have not been measured.
Bringing borrowing and investing together without hiding their differences.
Five financial products need to fit into one app, but borrowing and investing have different consequences. A simpler dashboard must still explain what a financial decision involves.
Product designer · 2025
I designed the shared dashboard, loan and investment journeys, and interface system across banking, borrowing, investments, insurance and payments.
The decisions behind the interface
Use one balance as the starting point. The dashboard places quick actions and pending tasks around a shared balance, with a reveal control for privacy.
Explain a loan before asking someone to request it. The empty state describes what borrowing is for and gives a clear Request Loan action instead of showing only a zero balance.
Show investment constraints before commitment. The minimum investment and wallet balance appear before the action. Projected values are labelled indicative and gross of withholding tax.
What was delivered
The design brings five financial products into a shared mobile system while keeping loan and investment decisions distinct.
The screens document the design approach. Interpretation of projections and risk language needs user testing; no financial or adoption results are claimed.

title: Reporting Portal
summary: Helping a project manager see what needs attention today.
text:
2025
Reporting Portal
Helping a project manager see what needs attention today.
My contribution
Dashboard concept
Designed dashboard coverage: four task states, four filter dimensions and two themes. Productivity outcomes are not yet measured.
Helping a project manager see what needs attention today.
A project count gives context, but it does not show what is due, at risk or waiting for review. Managers need an actionable view when they are scanning between meetings.
Product designer · 2025
I designed the reporting dashboard, task board, milestones, filters and responsive layouts in light and dark themes.
The decisions behind the interface
Put urgent work beside the totals. Tasks due, at-risk and critical work sit in the metrics row so the overview points toward an action.
Show tasks and milestones together. The board and upcoming milestones share a view, connecting day-to-day work to delivery dates.
Make review a visible state. To Do, In Progress, Review and Done are separate columns. Project, team, date and status filters help narrow the work without leaving the view.
What was delivered
The dashboard design combines four task states, four filter dimensions and two themes. The mobile layout preserves the key metrics and a focused board view.
The screens demonstrate information hierarchy and responsive behaviour. Faster issue resolution and productivity improvements have not been measured.

title: About Jamiu Abdulfatai
summary: Product designer working across fintech, AI products and complex workflows.
text:
Brighton, UK
00:00:00 UK
Jamiu Abdulfatai
UXUI | Product Designer
[Explore my work]
I design clear interfaces for payments, banking and complex workflows.
I work across web and mobile, from cross-border payments to banking across four subsidiaries. I’m studying MSc User Experience Design at the University of Brighton.
I’m usually drawn to the part of a product where things get complicated. That’s where I find the most interesting design problems.
[The person behind the work]
I like untangling the things that make digital products difficult to use. Sometimes that means questioning a business rule; sometimes it means finding a simpler way to explain what’s happening.
I enjoy the design process, but I also like understanding how things are built. It helps me make decisions that work beyond the Figma file, and gives me more useful conversations with engineers.
At Brighton, I’m developing my research practice and spending more time questioning the decisions behind interfaces, especially how research and AI can help us design more responsibly. My AI practice is part of that exploration.
When I’m not thinking about interfaces, there’s a good chance I’m somewhere playing football.

title: Design systems
summary: Design systems from Jamiu’s published portfolio.
text:
[The extended portfolio]
Design systems
Foundations, components & product systems
Design system
Colour
Ten-step ramps from 50 to 900 across primary, grey, success, danger, warning and info, plus black and white alpha scales for overlays and dividers.
Design system
Semantic styles, in the file
The published styles as they exist in Figma: Brand Primary, Neutral, Error, Warning and Success as groups, a Body to Header text scale, and Shadow Sm through XL.
Design system
Typeface
Inter, with the reasoning recorded - variable weights, tall x-height, tabular numerals and a slashed zero for interfaces that display figures. Credited to its maker in the sheet.
Design system
Elevation
A shadow scale used as depth hierarchy, so a dropdown, a card and a modal never sit at the same visual altitude.
Design system
Token naming
The colour and effect styles as named tokens - accent, dark and opacity tones on a numeric scale, with elevation as its own set.
Design system
Iconography
The icon set organised into semantic categories - navigation, actions, media, design tools - so an icon is chosen by meaning rather than by scrolling.
Design system
Icon grid
Stroke weight, bounding box and optical sizing held constant across the set.
Design system
Button group
Default, hover, focus, press, selected and disabled - crossed with giant, large and medium - plus segmented groups from five items down to two, and icon-only variants.
Design system
Input
Empty, placeholder, focused, filled, success and error, each with label and helper text, so validation is designed rather than bolted on.
Design system
Dropdown
Closed, open, selected and multi-select states with overflow behaviour.
Design system
Alert
Success, warning, error and information, with and without actions.
Design system
Card
Content, media and action layouts at each density.
Design system
List
Row anatomy - leading media, text block, trailing action, dividers and states.
Design system
Tabs
Underline and pill variants, with active, hover and disabled states.
Design system
Top navigation
Desktop and compact arrangements with search, actions and account.
Design system
Bottom navigation
Mobile bar at three, four and five items, with active and badged states.
Design system
Context menu
Grouped items, dividers, icons, shortcuts, submenus and destructive actions.
Design system
Action sheet
Mobile sheet with grouped and destructive actions and a cancel affordance.
Design system
Dialog
Confirmation, form and message dialogs with header, body and action rows.
Design system
Pagination
Numbered, truncated and compact variants with first, last and disabled edges.
Design system
Page control
Dot indicators at each count, with active and overflow handling.
Design system
Breadcrumbs
Depth, truncation and the current-page state.
Design system
Stepper
Incrementer with minimum, maximum and disabled bounds.
Design system
Progress
Determinate and indeterminate, with and without a value label.
Design system
Loader
Spinner sizes and placement rules for inline and blocking waits.
Design system
Toggle
On, off, focused and disabled at each size.
Design system
Radio
Selected, unselected, focused, disabled and error.
Design system
Avatar
Image, initial and fallback at each size, with status and grouped stacks.
Design system
Tooltip
Placement on all four sides with arrow alignment and overflow.
Design system
Bizinc - Local Deals, documented for front-end development
Handoff documentation rather than a component sheet: an overview, the components in play, numbered interaction specs, empty and error states, responsive behaviour across mobile and desktop, and a prototype link. Written so the build matches the design without a meeting.

Bizinc - Sidebar documentation
V2 sub-components: vertical menu item and sidebar button across default, hover, active and focused, the menu at six through two items, and the collapsed and expanded states of the whole shell.
Design system
Bizinc - Style guide
The product's own foundation: brand colour with hex values, a Poppins scale from H1 to small, and button variants annotated with border weights and fill rules for the developers building them.
Design system
Chalant AI - Navigation components
Badge, nav item, logo, button, avatar and sidebar, each with expanded and collapsed variants - and the sidebar resolved three times for the learner, trainer and admin roles from one component.
Design system
Bizinc - Layout grid, applied
The same page checked against the published web grid at three widths. Columns are a rule the layout is measured against, not a decoration.

Shortlet Lagos - Foundation and input states
Input documented through placeholder, typing, filled, success and error, alongside the iconography foundation - heroicons, specified at 2px stroke and a 24×24 box with usage rules.

title: AI practice
summary: Product UX, model evaluation and working prototypes.
text:
[AI practice]
Product design, model evaluation and working prototypes.
My interest in AI starts with what people actually need to do. At Kremor AI I worked on generated fashion, human review and the operational steps behind production. My evaluation work separately examined model output rather than treating it as user research.
Evaluate the output before designing around it.
At Kremor AI I worked across forensic benchmarking, dataset annotation and qualitative evaluation of LLM and generative-image output, covering complex AI interaction tasks. This was model evaluation alongside product design, not participant usability research.
Keep hypotheses separate from findings.
I use AI to explore options and organise research, then check the source material. I use official guidance to ground early models before testing them with people. I label what is sourced, what is hypothesised and what needs validation.
Output: what did the model produce?
Pattern: was the behaviour repeatable?
Risk: what happens when it is wrong?
Give people a first move.
For Kremor AI, I designed prompt scaffolding, conversational starting points and the connected storefront-to-production workflow. Five operational roles, confirmation gates, permissions and audit history make an open-ended AI experience more controllable.
Make judgement part of the task.
Chalantwork connects AI-assisted sustainability work to evidence and maker-checker review. Its live platform brings reporting and operational decisions into a governed workflow.
Connect conversation to a real task.
The Bizinc assistant-to-booking concept explores conversational discovery. It remains a proposal until business relevance, live availability and booking impact are validated.
The question I design around
Does the person know what the system did, what still needs their approval and what to do when the answer is wrong?
Make ideas testable.
My technical practice includes LangGraph for graph-based agent flows, Hugging Face for open-source model and agent integration, and React.js for front-end implementation awareness. These support the product design rather than replace it.
Academic Proofreader
I built a personal plugin experiment for careful academic editing: minimal changes, preserved citations and author approval before substantial rewrites. It returns edited text, significant changes and questions to review. It does not promise AI-detector scores.
Context before answers.
I built a page-aware portfolio agent that connects a visitor’s question to the current route, conversation context, project knowledge and supporting evidence. That work informs how I structure context for AI-assisted products.
Tools support the method.
I use Claude, ChatGPT, Codex and Google Antigravity around research synthesis, design exploration, functional prototypes and workflow automation, with human review before output becomes a claim or a shipped experience.
